backTranslations.41:
**Before the appointment**
- Add the appointment date in the Visit tab. MenoMap shows you how ready the notes are and what would make them stronger.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most. Limit yourself to three or four.
- Create the notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the appointment**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is designed to be readable in under a minute: counts, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and are not**

They are a summary of what you entered, plus anything you chose to bring from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis nor a complete medical record, and the patterns in them are coincidence checks, not proof of a cause. Your doctor may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add any new medication together with the date you started it. In a few weeks MenoMap can show you the records from before and after, which makes the next review easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day that marks 12 months in a row without a period, when this is not explained by something else (for example pregnancy, some medications or surgery). In many countries it occurs on average at a little over 50, but it is common any time between about 45 and 55.

**Perimenopause** is the period of years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall irregularly, so periods can become irregular, heavier, lighter, more frequent or less frequent. Many of the changes people associate with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep and mood changes, often begin in this stage, while periods still occur. Perimenopause can last a few years or even much longer and looks different for each person.

**Postmenopause** means everything that follows after this 12-month threshold. Some symptoms ease over time; others can continue for years.

Menopause can also occur earlier, because of surgery removing the ovaries, some cancer treatments or other conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency and is worth discussing with a doctor.

**How it is recognized.** In many people over 45, doctors recognize perimenopause or menopause based on history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always necessary, because hormone levels vary from day to day. They are more likely used when the person is younger or the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you what stage you are in. What it can do is keep an honest record of what you notice: flashes, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, often on the face, neck and chest, sometimes with flushing, sweating, a racing heartbeat or a chill afterwards. A night sweat is the same thing during sleep and can be so strong that it wakes you or wets your sheets.

They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people have a few, mild ones; others have many a day, which disrupt their work and sleep. In some they disappear within a few years; in others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** People often notice patterns linked to alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, heated rooms, stress or thick bedding. These vary a lot from person to person, which is why tracking your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes.** Flushing and sweating can also be caused by thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern or come together with weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, tell a doctor.

**How to describe them well.** Useful details for an appointment:
- How many you have per day and per night, roughly
- How strong they feel and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to come before them
- What you tried and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's Flash button and the later logging exist precisely to capture all this without much effort.

**Help exists.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, plus practical approaches. Which suit you is a conversation to have with a doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT, hormone replacement therapy, or MHT, menopause hormone therapy) replaces some of the estrogen that the body produces in smaller amounts around menopause. Major guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats in many people and it can also help with other symptoms.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms, such as dryness. People who still have a uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen together with the estrogen, to protect the lining of the uterus.

**Benefits and risks depend on the person:** age, how much time has passed since periods stopped, personal and family history (for example of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), as well as the type and route of administration of the treatment. That is why it is a decision to make together with a doctor who knows your history, not something an app can decide.

**Questions people often ask:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- What type and form would you recommend to me and why?
- What benefits might I expect and how quickly?
- What are my personal risks and how do they compare with no treatment?
- What should I watch for and when should we reassess the treatment?

**If you already take it,** record it in MenoMap (Profile → Medications). MenoMap will show you the flashes from before and after you started it, as a coincidence check and not as proof, so that you have something concrete to discuss at the review.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not right for everyone, and some people simply prefer other paths. There are several.

**Prescription options.** Some non-hormonal medications have evidence that they reduce hot flashes. Among them are certain medications originally developed for other conditions and a newer class designed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talking therapies and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause has evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes people find helpful:**
- Layers of clothes you can take off quickly
- A fan at the desk and by the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing and reducing personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help here)
- Regular exercise and a consistent sleep schedule

**Supplements and herbal products.** The evidence is contradictory or limited for many of them, quality varies, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter products.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own records from before and during a change, which is easier to judge than an impression.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short and it is hard to remember a month of nights on the spot. People tend to remember the most recent days or the hardest ones. A simple record fills the gap.

**What a diary gives your doctor:**
- How often symptoms occur and how strong they are, not only that they occur
- Whether things are improving, getting worse or staying the same
- What was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point to compare against if you try a treatment

**Keep it simple.** A diary helps only if you keep it. MenoMap is built around a one-tap Flash button and a four-question evening check-in, so it takes you a few seconds, not a whole notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of records usually show a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Visit tab helps you choose questions and prints them together with the notes.

backTranslations.479:
Once you have gone past 12 months without a period, **any vaginal bleeding must be checked by a doctor**, even if it occurred only once and even if it was only spotting or a light pink or brownish discharge.

Most of the time the cause turns out not to be serious. Thinning of the vaginal or uterine lining is common, for example. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when found early. That is why public health recommendations say to have it checked, instead of waiting.

**If you take hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns may be expected, depending on the type you take. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual or that occurs at the wrong time must also be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or health service and say that you have had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, how heavy it was and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can keep this information for you (Profile → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding occurred. It will remind you to have it checked by a doctor and will include it in the notes for the appointment.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints in midlife and rarely has a single cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly or leave you too hot or too wet to fall asleep.

**Other common factors:**
- Needing to urinate at night
- Anxiety or thoughts that will not stop
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but tends to fragment the second half of the night
- Caffeine consumed later in the day
- Pain, restless legs syndrome or a partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnea (worth mentioning, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What usually helps people.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layers of clothes you can take off; a consistent wake-up time; and less alcohol close to bedtime. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied approach, and many doctors can refer you to it.

**What to track.** For a week or two, note the sleep score, night flashes, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening check-in and flash log do this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show you sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app next to night sweats, as context, not as an explanation.

**When to get checked.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example, while driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or gasping at night.
